item.title: SQL Introduction
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Every app that remembers anything (your orders, messages, followers, progress through a course) stores that data in a database. SQL (Structured Query Language, often pronounced "sequel") is the language used to talk to most databases. It's one of the most useful and long-lasting skills in tech: developers, data analysts, product managers and marketers all use it.

What is a database?

A database is an organised collection of data that a program can search and update quickly and safely. The most common kind is a relational database, which stores data in tables, like spreadsheets:

  • Each row is one record (one customer).
  • Each column is one piece of information (name, city).
  • Tables can be related to each other: an orders table can point to the customer who placed each order. That's what "relational" means.

Why not just use a spreadsheet?

Databases are built for things spreadsheets struggle with:

  • Size: millions or billions of rows, still fast.
  • Many users at once: thousands of people placing orders at the same moment without overwriting each other.
  • Rules: every order must belong to a real customer; an email must be unique.
  • Safety: changes are saved reliably even if the server crashes mid-way.
  • Questions in code: "total sales per city last month" is one SQL statement.

Your first SQL query

SELECT name, city
FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Pune';

Read it like English: "Select the name and city from the customers table where the city is Pune." The database answers with a small table of results:

SQL is declarative: you describe what you want, and the database works out how to get it fast.

What SQL can do

SQL statements fall into a few groups:

  • Query data: SELECT (most of what you'll write).
  • Change data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
  • Define structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE.
  • Control access: GRANT, REVOKE (for administrators).

This course covers the first three groups.

Popular database systems

They all speak SQL. The core you'll learn here (SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY…) works the same in all of them; only small details differ, and we'll point them out.

SQL syntax basics

-- This is a comment
SELECT name FROM customers;   /* so is this */

select NAME from Customers;   -- keywords aren't case-sensitive
  • Statements end with a semicolon.
  • SQL keywords are not case-sensitive, but writing them in UPPER CASE is the common style and makes queries easier to read.
  • Text values go in single quotes: 'Pune'. (Double quotes are for column or table names in standard SQL.)
  • Spaces and new lines don't matter; spread long queries over several lines.
  • Whether table names and text comparisons are case-sensitive depends on the database system and its settings.

How to practise (free, nothing to install)

You need a database to run queries. The easiest options:

  1. sqliteonline.com or DB Fiddle (db-fiddle.com): run SQL in your browser. Choose SQLite, MySQL or PostgreSQL.
  2. DB Browser for SQLite: a free desktop app; the whole database is one file.
  3. Later, install MySQL or PostgreSQL locally, or use the database from your hosting panel (phpMyAdmin).

In the next lesson, you'll create the practice database used throughout this course with one copy-and-paste script.

Where SQL is used

  • Web development: every login, comment and product page reads from a database.
  • Data analysis: answering business questions from sales, traffic or app data.
  • Reporting tools like Looker Studio, Power BI and Metabase are built on SQL.
  • AI and data science: collecting and cleaning the data that models learn from.

Common mistakes

  • Double quotes around text values: use 'Pune', not "Pune" (MySQL allows both, PostgreSQL doesn't).
  • Forgetting the semicolon when running several statements.
  • Expecting rows in a particular order without asking for it (you'll learn ORDER BY).

Exercise

  1. Open sqliteonline.com (or any tool above) and run SELECT 1 + 1; to check it works.
  2. Run SELECT 'Hello, SQL!' AS greeting;.
  3. Think of an app you use daily. Write down three tables it probably has and three columns in each.

Summary

  • Relational databases store data in related tables of rows and columns.
  • SQL is the language for querying and changing that data; you say what you want, not how.
  • MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQLite all share the same core SQL.
  • Practise for free in the browser with sqliteonline.com or DB Fiddle.

Next, you'll create tables and load the practice database for this course.
item.excerpt:encoded: What databases and SQL are, why almost every app uses them, the main database systems, and how to practise SQL for free in your browser.

item.title: SQL Databases and Tables
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Before you can query data, it needs a home: a table with defined columns. In this lesson you'll learn how tables are created, choose data types, and set up the small online-shop database used for every example in the rest of the course.

Creating a table

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name    VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  city    VARCHAR(50),
  joined  DATE
);
  • CREATE TABLE customers creates a table named customers.
  • Inside the brackets, each line defines a column: its name, its data type, and optional rules.
  • PRIMARY KEY marks the column that uniquely identifies each row.
  • NOT NULL means the column must always have a value.

Common data types

Pick the type that matches the data: store prices in DECIMAL, not text, so you can add them up; store dates as DATE so you can sort and compare them. (SQLite is relaxed about types; MySQL and PostgreSQL enforce them.)

Write dates in the ISO format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. Every database understands it, and it sorts correctly.

Primary keys

Every table should have a primary key: a column (usually id) whose value is unique for every row and never empty. It's how other tables refer to a row, and how you update or delete exactly one record.

Databases can generate ids automatically:

-- MySQL
-- id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY

-- PostgreSQL
-- id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY      (or: id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY)

-- SQLite
-- id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY     (automatically increases)

NULL: the missing value

NULL means "no value / unknown". It's not zero and not an empty string. If a customer didn't tell you their city, city is NULL. You'll learn how to search for NULL in the WHERE lesson.

The practice database

Our shop has four related tables:

  • customers: who buys.
  • products: what we sell.
  • orders: one row per order, pointing to a customer.
  • order_items: which products (and how many) are in each order.

Copy this whole script into sqliteonline.com (or DB Fiddle with SQLite/MySQL/PostgreSQL) and run it:

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name    VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  email   VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE,
  city    VARCHAR(50),
  joined  DATE
);

CREATE TABLE products (
  id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  category  VARCHAR(50),
  price     DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
  stock     INTEGER DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  order_date   DATE NOT NULL,
  status       VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'pending'
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  product_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  qty         INTEGER NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

INSERT INTO customers (id, name, email, city, joined) VALUES
  (1, 'Asha',  'asha@example.com',  'Pune',   '2024-01-10'),
  (2, 'Rohan', 'rohan@example.com', 'Delhi',  '2024-02-03'),
  (3, 'Meera', 'meera@example.com', 'Jaipur', '2024-02-20'),
  (4, 'Kabir', 'kabir@example.com', 'Pune',   '2024-03-15'),
  (5, 'Sara',  NULL,                'Mumbai', '2024-04-01');

INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, stock) VALUES
  (1, 'Notebook',     'stationery',  120.00,  50),
  (2, 'Pen set',      'stationery',  250.00,  30),
  (3, 'Headphones',   'electronics', 1499.00, 0),
  (4, 'USB cable',    'electronics', 299.00,  75),
  (5, 'Backpack',     'bags',        1899.00, 12),
  (6, 'Water bottle', 'accessories', 350.00,  40),
  (7, 'Desk lamp',    'electronics', 899.00,  8);

INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, order_date, status) VALUES
  (1, 1, '2024-05-01', 'delivered'),
  (2, 2, '2024-05-03', 'delivered'),
  (3, 1, '2024-05-10', 'shipped'),
  (4, 3, '2024-05-12', 'pending'),
  (5, 4, '2024-05-15', 'delivered');

INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty) VALUES
  (1, 1, 3), (1, 2, 1),
  (2, 5, 1),
  (3, 4, 2),
  (4, 1, 5), (4, 6, 1),
  (5, 3, 1);

Check it worked:

SELECT * FROM products;

You should see 7 products. Keep this database open; every following lesson uses it. (If you close the browser tab, just run the script again.)

How the tables relate

customers (id) ──< orders (customer_id)
orders (id)    ──< order_items (order_id)
products (id)  ──< order_items (product_id)

One customer can have many orders; one order can have many items; one product can appear in many orders. Notice that Sara has no orders and the desk lamp has never been sold. These cases will matter when you learn JOINs.

Changing and removing tables

ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20);
-- DROP TABLE customers;   -- deletes the table and ALL its data. Be careful!

ALTER TABLE changes an existing table's structure. DROP TABLE deletes it permanently; there is no undo.

Naming conventions

  • Use lowercase names with underscores: order_items, customer_id.
  • Table names are usually plural (customers); column names singular.
  • Name foreign key columns <table>_id: customer_id.
  • Avoid spaces and reserved words like order, select or user as names.

Common mistakes

  • Storing numbers or dates as text, which breaks sorting and maths ("100" sorts before "20").
  • No primary key, making it impossible to target one row reliably.
  • Running DROP TABLE on real data without a backup.
  • Using reserved words like order as table names (that's why ours is orders).

Exercise

  1. Run the practice script and check each table with SELECT * FROM table_name;.
  2. Write a CREATE TABLE statement for a reviews table with id, product_id, rating (1–5), comment and created date.
  3. Add a phone column to customers with ALTER TABLE.

Summary

  • CREATE TABLE defines columns with names, data types and rules.
  • Choose proper types: INTEGER, DECIMAL, VARCHAR, DATE.
  • Every table needs a primary key; NULL means "no value".
  • The practice shop database (customers, products, orders, order_items) is used throughout the course.

Next, you'll read data from tables with SELECT.
item.excerpt:encoded: Create tables with CREATE TABLE, choose data types, understand primary keys and NULL, and load the practice shop database used in every lesson of this course.

item.title: SQL SELECT
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
SELECT is the statement you'll write more than any other. It reads data from one or more tables and returns a result table. This lesson covers the core of SELECT; the next lessons add filtering, sorting and grouping.

All examples use the practice shop database from the previous lesson.

Selecting all columns

SELECT * FROM customers;

* means "every column". The result has all 5 customers with id, name, email, city and joined date.

SELECT * is great for a quick look at a table. In application code, list the columns you need instead: it's faster, clearer, and doesn't break if someone adds a column later.

Selecting specific columns

SELECT name, city
FROM customers;

Columns appear in the order you list them.

Column aliases with AS

SELECT name AS customer, city AS location
FROM customers;

AS renames a column in the result (the table itself doesn't change). Aliases make results clearer and are essential for calculated columns. Use double quotes (or backticks in MySQL) if the alias has spaces: AS "Customer name".

Calculated columns

You can do maths and other operations right in the SELECT list:

SELECT name,
       price,
       price * 1.18 AS price_with_tax,
       stock,
       price * stock AS stock_value
FROM products;

The database calculates the new columns for every row. (How many decimals are shown depends on your database tool.)

Joining text

-- Standard SQL, PostgreSQL and SQLite:
SELECT name || ' from ' || city AS label FROM customers;

-- MySQL:
-- SELECT CONCAT(name, ' from ', city) AS label FROM customers;

Result: "Asha from Pune", "Rohan from Delhi"… CONCAT() also works in PostgreSQL and newer SQLite versions.

Removing duplicates with DISTINCT

SELECT city FROM customers;           -- Pune appears twice
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers;  -- each city once

DISTINCT applies to the whole row of selected columns: SELECT DISTINCT category, stock returns each unique combination.

SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products;

This gives the four categories: stationery, electronics, bags, accessories.

Limiting the number of rows

-- MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite:
SELECT name, price FROM products LIMIT 3;

-- Skip the first 3, then take 3 (page 2):
SELECT name, price FROM products LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;

-- SQL Server uses: SELECT TOP 3 name, price FROM products;

LIMIT is how websites show "10 results per page". Without ORDER BY (lesson 5), which rows you get first is not guaranteed, so always combine LIMIT with ORDER BY in real queries.

SELECT without a table

SELECT 2 + 3 AS answer, 'hello' AS word, CURRENT_DATE AS today;

Handy for testing expressions and functions.

Formatting long queries

SELECT
  name,
  category,
  price
FROM products;

One column per line, keywords on their own lines: easy to read and easy to comment out a single column with -- while testing.

How a SELECT is processed

Although you write SELECT first, the database logically does this:

  1. FROM: pick the table.
  2. WHERE: filter rows (next lesson).
  3. SELECT: choose and calculate columns.
  4. ORDER BY: sort.
  5. LIMIT: cut the result.

This explains why, for example, you can't use a column alias inside WHERE in most databases: WHERE runs before the alias is created.

Common mistakes

  • Comma after the last column: SELECT name, city, FROM customers is a syntax error.
  • Missing comma between columns: SELECT name city treats city as an alias for name!
  • SELECT * in application code.
  • Expecting a fixed order without ORDER BY.

Exercise

  1. Select the name and price of every product.
  2. Show each product's name and its price after a 10% discount, as sale_price.
  3. List each distinct order status in the orders table.
  4. Show the first 2 rows of order_items.
  5. Show customer names with their city in one column like "Asha (Pune)".

Summary

  • SELECT columns FROM table reads data; * means all columns.
  • AS renames result columns; you can calculate new columns with maths and text functions.
  • DISTINCT removes duplicate rows; LIMIT/OFFSET restrict and page results.
  • List columns explicitly in real code.

Next, you'll filter rows with WHERE.
item.excerpt:encoded: Read data with SELECT: choose columns, avoid SELECT * in real code, rename columns with AS, calculate new columns, remove duplicates with DISTINCT and limit results.

item.title: SQL WHERE
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Tables can have millions of rows, and you usually want only a few: orders from today, products under ₹500, customers in Pune. The WHERE clause filters rows so only those matching a condition are returned.

Basic WHERE

SELECT name, city
FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Pune';

The condition is checked for every row; only rows where it's true are kept.

Comparison operators

SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price < 500;

Returns Notebook (120), Pen set (250), USB cable (299) and Water bottle (350).

SELECT name, stock FROM products WHERE stock = 0;            -- out of stock: Headphones
SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE status <> 'delivered';   -- orders 3 and 4
SELECT name, joined FROM customers WHERE joined >= '2024-03-01'; -- Kabir and Sara

Dates in 'YYYY-MM-DD' format compare correctly.

AND, OR, NOT

-- Both conditions must be true
SELECT name, category, price
FROM products
WHERE category = 'electronics' AND price < 1000;

Returns USB cable and Desk lamp.

-- At least one condition must be true
SELECT name, city
FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Pune' OR city = 'Mumbai';

Returns Asha, Kabir and Sara.

-- NOT reverses a condition
SELECT name, category FROM products WHERE NOT category = 'electronics';

Use brackets with AND and OR

AND is evaluated before OR, which can give surprising results:

-- Intended: electronics or bags, but only under 1000
SELECT name, category, price
FROM products
WHERE category = 'electronics' OR category = 'bags' AND price < 1000;
-- Wrong! Read as: electronics OR (bags AND under 1000) → includes Headphones at 1499

SELECT name, category, price
FROM products
WHERE (category = 'electronics' OR category = 'bags') AND price < 1000;
-- Correct: USB cable and Desk lamp

Whenever you mix AND and OR, add brackets.

IN: match any value in a list

SELECT name, city
FROM customers
WHERE city IN ('Pune', 'Mumbai', 'Delhi');

Shorter and clearer than several ORs. NOT IN excludes the list.

BETWEEN: ranges

SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price BETWEEN 250 AND 900;

Returns Pen set (250), USB cable (299), Water bottle (350) and Desk lamp (899). BETWEEN includes both ends.

SELECT id, order_date
FROM orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-05-01' AND '2024-05-10';

Orders 1, 2 and 3. Careful with date-time columns: '2024-05-10' means midnight at the start of that day, so later times on the 10th are excluded. For timestamps, use >= '2024-05-01' AND < '2024-05-11'.

LIKE: text patterns

SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'Pen%';     -- starts with "Pen"
SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%lamp';    -- ends with "lamp"
SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%o%';      -- contains "o"
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE '_ara';    -- 4 letters ending "ara": Sara
  • % matches any number of characters (including none).
  • _ matches exactly one character.

Case sensitivity of LIKE differs: MySQL and SQLite usually ignore case for English letters; PostgreSQL is case-sensitive (use ILIKE there to ignore case).

LIKE '%word%' can't use an index (lesson 14), so it's slow on huge tables. Large sites use full-text search instead.

NULL needs IS NULL

SELECT name, email FROM customers WHERE email = NULL;   -- returns nothing!
SELECT name, email FROM customers WHERE email IS NULL;  -- Sara
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE email IS NOT NULL;     -- the other four

NULL means "unknown", and comparing anything with unknown gives unknown, never true, not even NULL = NULL. Always use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

This also affects <>: WHERE city <> 'Pune' does not return rows where city is NULL. Add OR city IS NULL if you want them.

Filtering on calculated values

SELECT name, price, stock, price * stock AS stock_value
FROM products
WHERE price * stock > 10000;

Returns Backpack (22,788), USB cable (22,425) and Water bottle (14,000). In most databases you must repeat the expression in WHERE rather than use the alias stock_value, because WHERE runs before SELECT.

Common mistakes

  • **= NULL** instead of IS NULL.
  • Double quotes around text: WHERE city = "Pune" fails in PostgreSQL.
  • Mixing AND/OR without brackets.
  • Forgetting that BETWEEN includes both ends, or that date-times on the end date are excluded.
  • Comparing numbers stored as text.

Exercise

  1. Find all products in the stationery category.
  2. Find products that cost more than ₹300 and have at least 10 in stock.
  3. Find customers who joined in February 2024.
  4. Find orders that are pending or shipped, using IN.
  5. Find products whose name contains the letter "e" and that cost under ₹500.
  6. Find customers without an email address.

Summary

  • WHERE keeps only rows that match a condition.
  • Use comparison operators, AND, OR, NOT and brackets to build conditions.
  • IN, BETWEEN and LIKE match lists, ranges and patterns.
  • Test for missing values with IS NULL, never = NULL.

Next, you'll sort results with ORDER BY.
item.excerpt:encoded: Filter rows with WHERE using comparison operators, AND, OR and NOT, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE patterns and IS NULL, and learn why NULL needs special handling.

item.title: SQL ORDER BY
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Without instructions, a database returns rows in whatever order is convenient for it, and that order can change. ORDER BY sorts the result exactly how you want: cheapest first, newest first, alphabetical.

Sorting ascending

SELECT name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price;

Ascending (smallest first, A→Z, oldest date first) is the default. You can write ASC to be explicit.

Sorting descending

SELECT name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC;

DESC reverses the order: most expensive first. Common uses: newest posts first (ORDER BY created_at DESC), highest scores first.

Sorting text and dates

SELECT name FROM customers ORDER BY name;                -- Asha, Kabir, Meera, Rohan, Sara
SELECT name, joined FROM customers ORDER BY joined DESC; -- newest members first: Sara first

Text is sorted alphabetically according to the database's collation (its rules for comparing text), which also decides whether uppercase and lowercase are treated the same.

Sorting by several columns

SELECT name, city
FROM customers
ORDER BY city, name;

The rows are sorted by city first; rows with the same city (Pune) are then sorted by name. Each column can have its own direction:

SELECT name, category, price
FROM products
ORDER BY category ASC, price DESC;

Categories A→Z, and inside each category, the most expensive product first.

Sorting by a calculated value or alias

SELECT name, price, stock, price * stock AS stock_value
FROM products
ORDER BY stock_value DESC;

Unlike WHERE, ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so you can use the alias. Backpack (22,788) comes first.

You can also sort by an expression that isn't in the SELECT list:

SELECT name FROM products ORDER BY LENGTH(name);   -- shortest names first

Sorting by column position (avoid)

SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY 2 DESC;  -- 2 = the second column (price)

This works but breaks silently if someone changes the column list. Use names.

Top-N queries with LIMIT

Combine ORDER BY with LIMIT to get "the top N":

-- The 3 most expensive products
SELECT name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC
LIMIT 3;

Backpack, Headphones, Desk lamp.

-- The most recent order
SELECT id, order_date
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_date DESC
LIMIT 1;

Order 5 (2024-05-15).

Pagination

-- Page 1: rows 1–3
SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY name LIMIT 3 OFFSET 0;
-- Page 2: rows 4–6
SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY name LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;

Always include ORDER BY when paging, or the same row could appear on two pages. Make the order unique too: if two rows tie, add the id as a tie-breaker, e.g. ORDER BY price DESC, id.

Where do NULLs go?

SELECT name, email FROM customers ORDER BY email;

Sara's NULL email appears first in MySQL and SQLite, but last in PostgreSQL (for ascending order). To control it:

-- PostgreSQL and SQLite 3.30+:
SELECT name, email FROM customers ORDER BY email NULLS LAST;

-- Works everywhere: sort by "is it null?" first
SELECT name, email
FROM customers
ORDER BY CASE WHEN email IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, email;

(CASE works like if/else inside SQL; you'll see it again later.)

Full query order so far

SELECT name, category, price
FROM products
WHERE stock > 0
ORDER BY price DESC
LIMIT 3;

The clauses must be written in this order: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Here: in-stock products only, most expensive first, top 3 → Backpack, Desk lamp, Water bottle.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting DESC for "newest" or "highest" queries.
  • LIMIT without ORDER BY, giving random-looking results.
  • Writing ORDER BY before WHERE.
  • Ties in pagination without a unique tie-breaker.

Exercise

  1. List all products from cheapest to most expensive.
  2. List customers alphabetically by city, then by name in reverse.
  3. Find the two products with the most stock.
  4. Show the oldest order.
  5. Show page 2 of products when sorted by name, with 2 products per page.

Summary

  • ORDER BY column sorts ascending; add DESC for descending.
  • Sort by several columns, each with its own direction, and by aliases or expressions.
  • Combine ORDER BY with LIMIT for top-N lists and pagination; add a tie-breaker.
  • NULL placement differs between databases; control it with NULLS LAST or CASE.

Next, you'll add new rows with INSERT.
item.excerpt:encoded: Sort query results with ORDER BY, ascending and descending, by several columns and by calculated values, handle NULLs, and get top-N results with LIMIT.

item.title: SQL INSERT
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
So far you've read data. Now you'll add it. Every sign-up, new post or order on a website ends in an INSERT statement.

Basic INSERT

INSERT INTO customers (id, name, email, city, joined)
VALUES (6, 'Neha', 'neha@example.com', 'Chennai', '2024-06-01');
  • INSERT INTO table (columns) lists the columns you're filling.
  • VALUES (…) gives the values in the same order.
  • Text and dates go in single quotes; numbers don't.

Check it:

SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = 6;

Always list the columns

You *can* leave out the column list:

INSERT INTO customers VALUES (7, 'Vikram', 'vikram@example.com', 'Kochi', '2024-06-02');

But then you must give a value for every column in the table's exact order. If someone later adds a column, this statement breaks (or worse, puts values in the wrong columns). Always list the columns explicitly.

Leaving columns out: NULL and DEFAULT

Columns you don't mention get their default value, or NULL if there's no default:

INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price)
VALUES (8, 'Sticky notes', 'stationery', 60);

SELECT name, stock FROM products WHERE id = 8;  -- stock is 0, the column's DEFAULT
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, order_date)
VALUES (6, 6, '2024-06-03');

SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE id = 6;     -- status is 'pending' (default)

A NOT NULL column without a default must be given a value, or the insert fails:

INSERT INTO products (id, category, price) VALUES (9, 'bags', 999);
-- Error: NOT NULL constraint failed: products.name

Auto-generated ids

In real apps you don't pick ids yourself; the database generates them. Leave the id out:

INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city, joined)
VALUES ('Isha', 'isha@example.com', 'Goa', '2024-06-05');

SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE email = 'isha@example.com';  -- gets the next id

This works because id is an auto-incrementing primary key (INTEGER PRIMARY KEY in SQLite, AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL, SERIAL/IDENTITY in PostgreSQL). Your application can then ask for the new id:

  • MySQL: SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();
  • SQLite: SELECT last_insert_rowid();
  • PostgreSQL: add RETURNING id to the INSERT.
-- PostgreSQL (and SQLite 3.35+):
-- INSERT INTO customers (name, city) VALUES ('Dev', 'Surat') RETURNING id;

Inserting several rows at once

INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty) VALUES
  (6, 1, 2),
  (6, 8, 4),
  (6, 6, 1);

One statement, many rows: much faster than separate statements when loading lots of data.

Copying rows with INSERT ... SELECT

You can insert the result of a query:

CREATE TABLE pune_customers (
  id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name  VARCHAR(100),
  email VARCHAR(100)
);

INSERT INTO pune_customers (id, name, email)
SELECT id, name, email
FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Pune';

SELECT * FROM pune_customers;  -- Asha and Kabir

Useful for archiving old data, building report tables or copying data between tables.

Constraint errors

The database protects your data using the rules you set when creating the table:

INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Fake Asha', 'asha@example.com');
-- Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: customers.email

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, order_date) VALUES (999, '2024-06-10');
-- Error in MySQL/PostgreSQL: foreign key violation (there's no customer 999)

These errors are good: they stop bad data from getting in. (SQLite only checks foreign keys after PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;.) You'll learn more in the Constraints lesson.

Quotes inside text

To store a single quote, write it twice:

INSERT INTO products (name, category, price) VALUES ('Kid''s lunchbox', 'accessories', 299);

SQL injection: the most important security rule

When your application inserts user input, never build the SQL by joining strings:

// DANGEROUS (pseudo-code)
sql = "INSERT INTO comments (text) VALUES ('" + userInput + "')"

If a user types '); DROP TABLE comments; --, they can run their own SQL. This attack is called SQL injection, and it's one of the most common ways websites get hacked.

Always use parameterised queries (prepared statements), where values are sent separately from the SQL:

// Safe: the ? is filled in by the database driver
sql = "INSERT INTO comments (text) VALUES (?)"
db.execute(sql, [userInput])

Every language has this: ? placeholders in Python's sqlite3 and in Node.js libraries, $1 in PostgreSQL drivers, PDO prepared statements in PHP, and $wpdb->prepare() in WordPress. You'll use this pattern in the Python course.

Common mistakes

  • Values in a different order from the column list.
  • Missing quotes around text or dates (or quotes around numbers, which some databases reject).
  • Setting ids by hand in real applications; let the database generate them.
  • Building SQL from user input with string concatenation.

Exercise

  1. Add yourself as a customer without giving an id. Find your new id.
  2. Add two new products in one INSERT statement.
  3. Create an order for your new customer and add two items to it.
  4. Try to insert a customer with an email that already exists and read the error.
  5. Create a table expensive_products and fill it with every product over ₹1000 using INSERT ... SELECT.

Summary

  • INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (…) adds a row; always list the columns.
  • Missing columns get their DEFAULT or NULL; let the database generate ids.
  • Insert many rows in one statement, or copy rows with INSERT ... SELECT.
  • Constraints reject bad data; parameterised queries prevent SQL injection.

Next, you'll change existing rows with UPDATE.
item.excerpt:encoded: Add rows with INSERT INTO, list columns explicitly, insert several rows at once, use defaults and auto-generated ids, copy rows with INSERT ... SELECT, and avoid SQL injection.

item.title: SQL UPDATE
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Data changes all the time: a customer moves city, a price goes up, an order is shipped. UPDATE changes values in existing rows. It's simple to write, and also the statement most likely to cause an accident, so this lesson covers safety habits too.

Basic UPDATE

UPDATE customers
SET city = 'Bengaluru'
WHERE id = 2;

SELECT name, city FROM customers WHERE id = 2;  -- Rohan, Bengaluru
  • UPDATE table names the table.
  • SET column = value gives the new value.
  • WHERE chooses which rows to change.

The golden rule: never forget WHERE

-- DON'T RUN THIS
-- UPDATE customers SET city = 'Bengaluru';

Without WHERE, every row in the table is updated. All your customers now live in Bengaluru, and there's no undo button. This mistake has hurt many real companies.

Safe habits:

  1. Write the WHERE clause first, then the SET part.
  2. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE before updating, to see exactly which rows will change:
SELECT * FROM products WHERE category = 'stationery';
-- Looks right? Now:
UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.10 WHERE category = 'stationery';
  1. Target rows by primary key (WHERE id = 2) when you mean one specific row; names and emails can be duplicated or mistyped.

Updating several columns

UPDATE products
SET price = 1299, stock = 25
WHERE id = 3;

Separate the assignments with commas.

Calculated updates

The new value can use the current values:

-- Restock: add 10 to the headphones' stock
UPDATE products SET stock = stock + 10 WHERE id = 3;

-- 10% discount on all electronics
UPDATE products SET price = price * 0.90 WHERE category = 'electronics';

-- Text changes
UPDATE products SET name = UPPER(name) WHERE id = 8;

stock = stock + 10 reads the value before the update, adds 10 and stores the result. For counters (likes, views, stock), this is safer than reading the value in your application and writing it back, because two users updating at once won't overwrite each other.

Updating many rows on purpose

UPDATE orders
SET status = 'delivered'
WHERE status = 'shipped' AND order_date < '2024-05-20';

Most tools report how many rows were changed ("1 row affected"). If that number surprises you, investigate.

Setting a value to NULL

UPDATE customers SET email = NULL WHERE id = 4;

Note: in SET, = assigns (so = NULL is correct here). It's only in WHERE that you need IS NULL.

Conditional values with CASE

UPDATE products
SET category = CASE
  WHEN price >= 1000 THEN 'premium'
  ELSE category
END
WHERE category = 'electronics';

CASE WHEN … THEN … ELSE … END chooses a value per row, like an if/else.

Updating using another table

Sometimes the new value depends on another table. A portable way uses a subquery (a query inside a query):

-- Mark customers who have at least one order as 'active'
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'new';

UPDATE customers
SET status = 'active'
WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);

SELECT name, status FROM customers;

Everyone except Sara (and any customers you added without orders) becomes active. MySQL and PostgreSQL also have UPDATE … JOIN / UPDATE … FROM syntax for this.

Transactions: an undo button

A transaction groups statements so they either all happen or none do. Until you COMMIT, you can ROLLBACK:

BEGIN;

UPDATE products SET price = price * 2;   -- oops, forgot WHERE!
SELECT name, price FROM products;        -- everything doubled

ROLLBACK;                                -- undo everything since BEGIN

SELECT name, price FROM products;        -- back to normal

When everything looks right, use COMMIT; instead of ROLLBACK; to save the changes permanently.

Transactions are essential for operations that must happen together, like moving money:

BEGIN;
-- UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
-- UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;

If anything fails between the two updates, a rollback ensures money is never lost or created. (Some tools and settings commit automatically after each statement unless you start a transaction with BEGIN.)

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting WHERE. Every row changes.
  • **Using IS NULL in SET** or = NULL in WHERE (the opposite of correct).
  • Updating by name when names aren't unique.
  • Read-modify-write in application code for counters, instead of SET x = x + 1.
  • Big updates on live data without a transaction or backup.

Exercise

  1. Change Meera's city to "Udaipur". Check the result with SELECT first and after.
  2. Increase the price of all stationery by 5%.
  3. Set the stock of the out-of-stock product to 20.
  4. Inside a transaction, set every order to 'cancelled', look at the result, then roll back.
  5. Mark order 4 as 'shipped'.

Summary

  • UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE condition changes existing rows.
  • Without WHERE, every row changes: write WHERE first and test it with SELECT.
  • Values can be calculated from current values (stock = stock + 10) or chosen with CASE.
  • Transactions (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK) make changes all-or-nothing and undoable.

Next, you'll remove rows with DELETE.
item.excerpt:encoded: Change existing rows with UPDATE and SET, always target rows with WHERE, update several columns and calculated values, and use transactions as a safety net.

item.title: SQL DELETE
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
DELETE removes rows from a table. Like UPDATE, it's easy to write and easy to get badly wrong, so you'll learn the safe way to use it, and when not to delete at all.

Basic DELETE

DELETE FROM pune_customers
WHERE id = 4;

SELECT * FROM pune_customers;  -- only Asha is left

(pune_customers is the copy table from the INSERT lesson. If you don't have it, practise on any test table.)

  • DELETE FROM table names the table.
  • WHERE chooses which rows to remove.

The golden rule, again: WHERE

-- DON'T RUN THIS ON REAL DATA
-- DELETE FROM customers;

Without WHERE, every row is deleted. The table stays, but it's empty. Use the same habits as UPDATE:

  1. Write and run a SELECT with the WHERE clause first.
  2. Check the number of rows.
  3. Change SELECT * to DELETE and run it, ideally inside a transaction.
SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 6;  -- check
BEGIN;
DELETE FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 6;
-- check the result, then:
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK;

Deleting several rows

DELETE FROM products
WHERE stock = 0 AND category = 'electronics';

Any condition that works in SELECT works in DELETE: IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, subqueries.

-- Remove items that belong to cancelled orders
DELETE FROM order_items
WHERE order_id IN (SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled');

Foreign keys protect related data

What happens if you delete a customer who has orders?

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;   -- SQLite only: turn on foreign key checks

DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 1;
-- Error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed

Asha has orders that point to her id. Deleting her would leave "orphaned" orders that belong to nobody, so the database refuses. (MySQL with InnoDB and PostgreSQL check foreign keys automatically.)

You decide what should happen when you create the table:

-- customer_id INTEGER REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
--   deleting a customer also deletes their orders

-- customer_id INTEGER REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
--   their orders stay, with customer_id set to NULL

-- (default) ON DELETE RESTRICT / NO ACTION
--   the delete is refused while related rows exist

CASCADE is convenient but powerful: one DELETE can remove thousands of related rows. Use it deliberately. You'll see more in the Constraints and Keys lesson.

DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP

TRUNCATE (not available in SQLite) is used to empty big tables quickly, for example log or test tables. In MySQL it also resets the auto-increment counter and can't be rolled back. DROP removes the table completely.

Soft deletes: often better than deleting

Many applications never really delete important data. Instead, they mark it as deleted:

ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN deleted_at TIMESTAMP;

-- "Delete" a product
UPDATE products SET deleted_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE id = 8;

-- Normal queries ignore deleted products
SELECT name FROM products WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

-- Restore it
UPDATE products SET deleted_at = NULL WHERE id = 8;

Benefits:

  • Mistakes can be undone.
  • Old orders still show the product they contained.
  • You keep history for reports and audits.

WordPress does this with its Trash: a trashed post has post_status = 'trash' until it's permanently deleted.

The downside: every query needs WHERE deleted_at IS NULL, and privacy laws may require truly deleting personal data when a user asks. Many apps soft-delete first, then permanently delete after 30 days.

Backups

The real safety net is a backup. Before big changes on a live site, export the database (Hostinger's panel, phpMyAdmin's Export, or mysqldump). If something goes wrong, you can restore it.

Common mistakes

  • DELETE without WHERE.
  • Not checking with SELECT first.
  • Surprise cascades: deleting one row removes much more than expected.
  • Deleting data you need for history (old orders, invoices) instead of soft-deleting.
  • Thinking DELETE frees disk space immediately: databases often reuse the space later rather than shrinking the file.

Exercise

  1. Create a test table, insert five rows, then delete two of them with one statement.
  2. With foreign keys on, try to delete a customer who has orders. Read the error.
  3. Delete the order items of order 6 inside a transaction, check, then roll back.
  4. Add a deleted_at column to a test table, soft-delete one row, and write a SELECT that hides it.

Summary

  • DELETE FROM table WHERE condition removes rows; without WHERE it removes all of them.
  • Always SELECT first and use transactions for important deletes.
  • Foreign keys refuse, cascade or nullify deletes of related rows, depending on your rules.
  • TRUNCATE empties a table fast; DROP removes it; soft deletes keep data recoverable.

Next, you'll summarise data with aggregate functions like COUNT, SUM and AVG.
item.excerpt:encoded: Remove rows with DELETE safely, understand how foreign keys protect related data, compare DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP, and when to use soft deletes instead.

item.title: SQL Functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG)
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Often you don't want a list of rows but an answer: How many customers do we have? What's the average price? When was the last order? Aggregate functions calculate one value from many rows. SQL also has many scalar functions that work on one value at a time, for text, numbers and dates.

The examples use the original practice data from lesson 2. If you've changed it in the last lessons, re-run the setup script for matching results.

COUNT

SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers FROM customers;   -- 5

COUNT(*) counts rows. Combine it with WHERE:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS pune_customers FROM customers WHERE city = 'Pune';  -- 2

COUNT(column) ignores NULL

SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows,
       COUNT(email) AS with_email
FROM customers;

COUNT(column) only counts rows where that column is not NULL. Sara has no email, so she isn't counted.

COUNT(DISTINCT …)

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS cities FROM customers;  -- 4 (Pune counted once)
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS buyers FROM orders;  -- 4 customers have ordered

SUM

SELECT SUM(stock) AS units_in_stock FROM products;           -- 215
SELECT SUM(price * stock) AS inventory_value FROM products;  -- 79905

SUM adds up numbers. You can sum an expression, like price × stock for each row.

AVG

SELECT AVG(price) AS average_price FROM products;   -- about 759.43
SELECT ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS average_price FROM products;

AVG calculates the mean. ROUND(value, 2) keeps 2 decimals.

NULLs are ignored by SUM and AVG too. If some products had a NULL price, AVG would divide by the number of products with a price. Usually that's what you want, but be aware of it.

MIN and MAX

SELECT MIN(price) AS cheapest, MAX(price) AS most_expensive FROM products;  -- 120, 1899
SELECT MIN(order_date) AS first_order, MAX(order_date) AS latest_order FROM orders;

MIN and MAX work on numbers, dates and text (alphabetically first/last).

Several aggregates at once

SELECT COUNT(*)              AS products,
       SUM(stock)            AS units,
       ROUND(AVG(price), 2)  AS avg_price,
       MIN(price)            AS min_price,
       MAX(price)            AS max_price
FROM products
WHERE category = 'electronics';

A one-row summary of the electronics category.

You can't mix aggregates with normal columns (yet)

SELECT name, MAX(price) FROM products;

This asks for one value (MAX) and a column with 7 values at the same time. PostgreSQL and strict MySQL return an error; SQLite returns a result but it's easy to misread. To find which product is the most expensive, sort and limit:

SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 1;

To get aggregates per group (per category, per city), you need GROUP BY, the next lesson.

Useful text functions

SELECT UPPER(name)          AS upper_name,
       LOWER(email)         AS lower_email,
       LENGTH(name)         AS name_length,
       SUBSTR(name, 1, 3)   AS first_three,
       TRIM('  hi  ')       AS trimmed,
       REPLACE(city, 'Pune', 'Poona') AS old_name
FROM customers;
  • SUBSTR(text, start, length) (SUBSTRING in some databases) starts counting at 1.
  • Text joining: || in PostgreSQL/SQLite, CONCAT() in MySQL.

Number functions

SELECT ROUND(1499 * 1.18, 2) AS with_tax,   -- 1768.82
       ROUND(17.5)           AS rounded,     -- 18
       ABS(-42)              AS absolute,    -- 42
       10 % 3                AS remainder;   -- 1 (MOD(10, 3) in some databases)

Also CEIL/CEILING and FLOOR in MySQL and PostgreSQL.

Handling NULL with COALESCE

SELECT name, COALESCE(email, 'no email') AS contact
FROM customers;

COALESCE(a, b, …) returns the first value that isn't NULL. Perfect for display defaults, and for treating NULL as 0 in calculations: COALESCE(discount, 0).

Date functions

Date functions differ the most between databases:

-- SQLite: month of each order
SELECT id, order_date, STRFTIME('%m', order_date) AS month FROM orders;

-- Customers who joined in the last 30 days (MySQL):
-- SELECT name FROM customers WHERE joined >= CURDATE() - INTERVAL 30 DAY;

CURRENT_DATE and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP work in all three.

CASE: if/else in a query

SELECT name, price,
       CASE
         WHEN price < 300 THEN 'budget'
         WHEN price < 1000 THEN 'mid-range'
         ELSE 'premium'
       END AS price_band
FROM products;

CASE is the Swiss Army knife of SQL: labels, custom sorting, and conditional counting:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS total,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS delivered
FROM orders;   -- 5 total, 3 delivered

Common mistakes

  • **Expecting COUNT(column) to count NULLs.**
  • Mixing aggregates and plain columns without GROUP BY.
  • Integer division: in PostgreSQL and SQLite, 7 / 2 is 3. Use 7.0 / 2 or CAST for decimals.
  • Copying date functions between databases without checking.

Exercise

  1. Count how many orders have the status 'delivered'.
  2. Find the total number of items sold (sum of qty in order_items).
  3. Find the average price of stationery, rounded to 2 decimals.
  4. Find the earliest and latest customer join dates.
  5. Show every customer's name and email, with "–" where the email is missing.
  6. Label each product's stock as 'out', 'low' (under 20) or 'ok'.

Summary

  • COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX turn many rows into one value.
  • COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column), SUM and AVG ignore NULLs.
  • Text, number and date functions transform single values; date functions vary by database.
  • COALESCE replaces NULLs; CASE adds if/else logic.

Next, you'll calculate aggregates per group with GROUP BY.
item.excerpt:encoded: Summarise data with aggregate functions COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX, understand how they treat NULL, and use common text, number and date functions.

item.title: SQL GROUP BY
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Aggregate functions give you one answer for the whole table. GROUP BY gives you one answer per group: products per category, orders per customer, sales per month. It's the heart of every report and dashboard.

Grouping by one column

SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS products
FROM products
GROUP BY category;

How it works:

  1. The database puts rows with the same category into groups.
  2. It runs COUNT(*) separately for each group.
  3. It returns one row per group.

Several aggregates per group

SELECT category,
       COUNT(*)             AS products,
       SUM(stock)           AS units,
       ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS avg_price,
       MAX(price)           AS top_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY units DESC;

The rule for SELECT with GROUP BY

Every column in SELECT must either be in the GROUP BY or inside an aggregate function.

-- Wrong: which product name should represent the whole category?
-- SELECT category, name, COUNT(*) FROM products GROUP BY category;

Each group has several names, so there's no single answer. PostgreSQL and strict MySQL give an error; SQLite silently picks one, which is misleading. Group by the columns you want to show.

Grouping by several columns

SELECT customer_id, status, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id, status
ORDER BY customer_id;

One row per unique combination of customer and status.

Grouping order items

SELECT order_id,
       COUNT(*) AS lines,
       SUM(qty) AS units
FROM order_items
GROUP BY order_id;

To add order totals in rupees, you need prices from the products table. That's a JOIN, coming in the next lesson.

Grouping by a calculated value

-- SQLite: orders per month
SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY month;

-- MySQL:      GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m')
-- PostgreSQL: GROUP BY TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY-MM')
SELECT CASE WHEN price < 500 THEN 'under 500' ELSE '500 and up' END AS band,
       COUNT(*) AS products
FROM products
GROUP BY band;

Most databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite) let you GROUP BY a SELECT alias; in others, repeat the expression.

WHERE vs HAVING

  • WHERE filters rows before grouping.
  • HAVING filters groups after aggregating.
-- Categories with more than one product
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS products
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

electronics (3) and stationery (2).

You can't use WHERE here, because the count doesn't exist until after grouping.

Both together:

-- Among products in stock, categories whose average price is over 300
SELECT category, ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
WHERE stock > 0                 -- rows: drop out-of-stock products first
GROUP BY category
HAVING AVG(price) > 300         -- groups: keep expensive categories
ORDER BY avg_price DESC;

Electronics averages 599 here, not 899, because the out-of-stock headphones were removed by WHERE before grouping.

Customers with more than one order

SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;

Customer 1 (Asha) with 2 orders. A classic "loyal customers" query.

The full logical order of a query

You write clauses in this order:

SELECT … FROM … WHERE … GROUP BY … HAVING … ORDER BY … LIMIT …

The database logically processes them in this order:

  1. FROM: get the rows (and join tables).
  2. WHERE: filter rows.
  3. GROUP BY: form groups.
  4. HAVING: filter groups.
  5. SELECT: calculate output columns and aliases.
  6. ORDER BY: sort.
  7. LIMIT: cut.

Knowing this order explains most "why doesn't this work?" moments, for example why WHERE can't use an aggregate.

Common mistakes

  • Selecting a column that isn't grouped or aggregated.
  • Using WHERE for aggregate conditions (WHERE COUNT(*) > 1); use HAVING.
  • Using HAVING for row conditions that belong in WHERE; it works but is slower and less clear.
  • Forgetting ORDER BY: grouped results aren't guaranteed to be sorted.

Exercise

  1. Count customers per city, most customers first.
  2. Show the total stock and number of products per category, only for categories with at least 50 units.
  3. Count orders per status.
  4. In order_items, find products (by product_id) that were ordered more than once in total quantity.
  5. Count how many products fall into 'budget' (<300), 'mid' (300–999) and 'premium' (1000+) bands.

Summary

  • GROUP BY makes one result row per group; aggregates are calculated per group.
  • Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated.
  • WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after.
  • Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.

Next, you'll combine tables with INNER JOIN.
item.excerpt:encoded: Calculate totals per category, per customer and per month with GROUP BY, filter groups with HAVING, and understand the full order in which a query runs.

item.title: SQL JOINs (INNER JOIN)
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Our data is split across tables: orders store a customer_id, not the customer's name; order items store a product_id, not the price. A JOIN combines rows from related tables so you can see everything together. JOINs are what make relational databases powerful.

Why data is split

If every order row repeated the customer's name, email and city, then changing a customer's email would mean updating every one of their orders, and a missed one would leave inconsistent data. Instead, each fact is stored once, and tables point to each other with ids. This idea is called normalisation. JOINs put the pieces back together when you query.

Your first INNER JOIN

SELECT orders.id, orders.order_date, customers.name
FROM orders
INNER JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;
  • FROM orders starts with the orders table.
  • INNER JOIN customers adds the customers table.
  • ON orders.customer_id = customers.id says how rows match: an order belongs to the customer whose id equals the order's customer_id.
  • table.column says which table a column comes from. It's required when both tables have a column with the same name (both have id).

The word INNER is optional: a plain JOIN means INNER JOIN.

What "inner" means

An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables. Sara has no orders, so she doesn't appear. The desk lamp has never been ordered, so it won't appear in a join with order items. To include rows without matches, you'll use LEFT JOIN in the next lesson.

Table aliases

Writing full table names gets long. Give each table a short alias:

SELECT o.id, o.order_date, o.status, c.name, c.city
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.city = 'Pune'
ORDER BY o.order_date;

Asha's two orders and Kabir's one. (AS is optional for table aliases: FROM orders o.) Aliases like o and c are standard practice in every real codebase.

Joining three tables

Which products are in each order? order_items connects orders and products:

SELECT oi.order_id, p.name AS product, oi.qty, p.price
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
ORDER BY oi.order_id;

Add the customer with a third join:

SELECT c.name AS customer, o.id AS order_id, p.name AS product, oi.qty
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c    ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p     ON oi.product_id = p.id
ORDER BY c.name, o.id;

Each JOIN adds one table and one matching rule. Read it as a chain: customers ← orders → order_items → products.

JOIN + GROUP BY: real reports

Now you can calculate what you couldn't before: the value of each order.

SELECT o.id AS order_id,
       SUM(oi.qty * p.price) AS order_total
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY o.id
ORDER BY order_total DESC;

Total spent per customer:

SELECT c.name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.id)  AS orders,
       SUM(oi.qty * p.price) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;

Note COUNT(DISTINCT o.id): after joining items, Asha's first order appears on two rows (two products), so a plain COUNT(*) would count 3 "orders" for her instead of 2. Watch for this row multiplication whenever you join a one-to-many relationship and then aggregate.

Best-selling products by units:

SELECT p.name, SUM(oi.qty) AS units_sold
FROM products p
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY units_sold DESC;

The notebook leads with 8 units.

JOIN with extra conditions

Filter joined results with WHERE as usual:

SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status <> 'delivered';

Asha (order 3, shipped) and Meera (order 4, pending).

Ambiguous columns

-- SELECT id, name FROM orders JOIN customers ON customer_id = customers.id;
-- Error: ambiguous column name: id

Both tables have id, so the database doesn't know which you mean. Always prefix columns with the table alias in joins, even when not strictly required: it makes queries clearer.

Common mistakes

  • Missing or wrong ON condition: joining o.id = c.id instead of o.customer_id = c.id gives nonsense that looks plausible.
  • Forgetting a join condition entirely, which matches every row with every row (a "Cartesian product": 5 orders × 5 customers = 25 rows).
  • Counting rows after a one-to-many join; use COUNT(DISTINCT …).
  • Ambiguous column names without table prefixes.

Exercise

  1. List every order with the customer's name and city.
  2. List all products bought by Asha.
  3. Show each order's id, date, customer name and number of items.
  4. Find the total revenue from delivered orders only.
  5. Find each city's total sales.

Summary

  • JOIN table ON condition combines rows from related tables.
  • INNER JOIN keeps only rows with a match in both tables.
  • Use short aliases and prefix every column in joins.
  • JOIN + GROUP BY produces real reports; watch for row multiplication when counting.

Next, you'll keep rows without matches using LEFT JOIN.
item.excerpt:encoded: Combine rows from related tables with INNER JOIN, use table aliases, join three or four tables, and build real reports like order totals per customer.

item.title: SQL LEFT JOIN
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
An INNER JOIN drops rows that have no match. Often, that's exactly the data you want: customers who have never ordered, products nobody bought, posts with zero comments. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the first table, matched or not.

LEFT JOIN

SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.order_date
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY c.name;

Every customer from the left table (the one in FROM) appears. Where there's no matching order, the order columns are filled with NULL. Sara is now included.

Compare with INNER JOIN, which returned the same rows except Sara.

Finding rows with no match

The most common use: find what's missing. Keep the LEFT JOIN, then filter on NULL in the right table:

-- Customers who have never ordered
SELECT c.name, c.city
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

Sara (Mumbai). Perfect for a "send a welcome discount" email list.

-- Products that have never been sold
SELECT p.name, p.stock
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE oi.product_id IS NULL;

Only the desk lamp has never sold. Maybe it needs a better photo or a lower price.

Counting with zeros

INNER JOIN reports leave out the zeros. LEFT JOIN includes them:

SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY orders DESC, c.name;

Important: use COUNT(o.id), not COUNT(*). For Sara there's still one row (with NULLs), so COUNT(*) would say 1. COUNT(o.id) counts only non-NULL order ids, giving the correct 0.

Sums with COALESCE

SELECT p.name,
       COALESCE(SUM(oi.qty), 0) AS units_sold
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY units_sold DESC;

The desk lamp shows 0 instead of NULL, because SUM of nothing is NULL and COALESCE turns it into 0.

WHERE vs ON with LEFT JOIN

This is the trickiest part of LEFT JOIN. Compare:

-- A: condition in WHERE
SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered';
-- B: condition in ON
SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'delivered';
  • A returns only Rohan, Asha and Kabir with their delivered orders. The WHERE runs after the join and removes rows where o.status is NULL, so Sara and Meera disappear: the LEFT JOIN has effectively become an INNER JOIN.
  • B returns all five customers: those with a delivered order show it; Meera and Sara show NULLs.

Rule: conditions on the right table go in ON if you want to keep all left rows. Conditions on the left table go in WHERE.

Order of tables matters

A LEFT JOIN B keeps all of A. B LEFT JOIN A keeps all of B. Start FROM the table whose rows you want to keep completely.

RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN

-- RIGHT JOIN keeps all rows of the right table:
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM orders o
RIGHT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;
-- Same result as: customers LEFT JOIN orders

RIGHT JOIN is just a LEFT JOIN written backwards. Most developers always use LEFT JOIN and order the tables accordingly; it's easier to read. (SQLite added RIGHT JOIN in version 3.39.)

FULL OUTER JOIN keeps all rows from both tables, with NULLs on either side where there's no match. It's supported by PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite 3.39+, but not MySQL. It's mostly used for comparing two lists, e.g. reconciling two systems.

Self join

A table can be joined to itself with two aliases. For example, customers from the same city:

SELECT a.name AS customer, b.name AS neighbour, a.city
FROM customers a
JOIN customers b ON a.city = b.city AND a.id < b.id;

Asha and Kabir (both Pune). a.id < b.id avoids pairing someone with themselves and listing each pair twice. Self joins are also used for hierarchies, like an employees table where manager_id points to another employee.

Join types at a glance

Common mistakes

  • Filtering the right table in WHERE, which silently turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
  • **COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(right.id)**, giving 1 instead of 0.
  • Forgetting COALESCE, showing NULL instead of 0 in reports.
  • Putting the "keep all" table on the wrong side.

Exercise

  1. List all products with the total quantity sold, including 0 for unsold products.
  2. Find customers who have never ordered.
  3. Show every customer with the number of delivered orders (0 if none). Hint: put the status condition in ON.
  4. List every order with the number of items in it, including orders with no items. (Insert an empty order first to test.)
  5. Find pairs of products in the same category with a self join.

Summary

  • LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills missing matches with NULL.
  • WHERE right.id IS NULL finds rows without a match.
  • Use COUNT(right.id) and COALESCE(SUM(...), 0) for correct zeros.
  • Conditions on the right table belong in ON to keep all left rows.

Next, you'll protect your data with constraints and keys.
item.excerpt:encoded: Keep every row from the first table with LEFT JOIN, find rows without matches, count zero values correctly, and meet RIGHT, FULL and self joins.

item.title: SQL Constraints and Keys
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Application code has bugs, users type strange things, and scripts get run twice. Constraints are rules the database itself enforces, so bad data can't get in no matter where it comes from. They're your last and strongest line of defence for data quality.

The constraints

A table with every constraint

CREATE TABLE reviews (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  rating      INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
  comment     TEXT,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  UNIQUE (product_id, customer_id)
);

Read it rule by rule:

  • Every review has a unique id.
  • It must point to a real product and a real customer.
  • The rating is required and must be 1–5.
  • The comment is optional.
  • created_at fills itself in.
  • A customer can review each product only once (the pair must be unique).
  • If a product is deleted, its reviews are deleted with it.

Testing the rules

Turn on foreign keys if you're using SQLite, then try some inserts:

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;  -- SQLite only

INSERT INTO reviews (product_id, customer_id, rating, comment)
VALUES (1, 1, 5, 'Great paper quality');           -- OK

INSERT INTO reviews (product_id, customer_id, rating)
VALUES (1, 2, 7);                                  -- CHECK fails: rating must be 1–5

INSERT INTO reviews (product_id, customer_id, rating)
VALUES (1, 1, 4);                                  -- UNIQUE fails: Asha already reviewed product 1

INSERT INTO reviews (product_id, customer_id, rating)
VALUES (99, 1, 4);                                 -- FOREIGN KEY fails: no product 99

INSERT INTO reviews (product_id, customer_id)
VALUES (2, 1);                                     -- NOT NULL fails: rating is required

Each bad insert is rejected with an error explaining which rule failed. Your application can catch these errors and show a friendly message.

Primary keys

  • Exactly one per table; values unique and never NULL.
  • Usually a meaningless number (id) generated by the database. Don't use real-world values like email or phone as primary keys: people change them.
  • A composite primary key uses several columns, like PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id) in order_items: each product appears at most once per order.

Foreign keys

A foreign key links a column to the primary key of another table:

-- customer_id INTEGER REFERENCES customers(id)
-- or, as a separate line:
-- FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id)

It guarantees referential integrity: every order belongs to a customer who exists. Without it, deleting customers would leave orphaned orders pointing at nothing.

ON DELETE options

Choose per relationship:

  • Reviews of a deleted product → CASCADE (they're meaningless alone).
  • Orders of a deleted customer → RESTRICT (keep financial records; deactivate the customer instead).
  • Posts by a deleted author → SET NULL (keep the posts, show "former author").

There's also ON UPDATE CASCADE, rarely needed when ids never change.

UNIQUE

-- email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE

Guarantees no duplicates, e.g. one account per email. It's much safer than checking in application code ("is this email taken?") because two sign-ups at the same instant could both pass the check. The database never lets both through.

Most databases allow several NULLs in a UNIQUE column, since NULL means "unknown". That's why Sara (no email) doesn't conflict with anyone.

CHECK

-- price DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (price >= 0)
-- status VARCHAR(20) CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled'))
-- CHECK (end_date >= start_date)

Any condition on the row's own values. (MySQL enforces CHECK from version 8.0.16; older versions ignored it.)

Adding constraints to existing tables

-- MySQL / PostgreSQL:
-- ALTER TABLE products ADD CONSTRAINT price_positive CHECK (price >= 0);
-- ALTER TABLE customers ADD CONSTRAINT email_unique UNIQUE (email);

Adding a constraint fails if existing data already breaks it, so clean the data first. (SQLite has limited ALTER TABLE support; there you usually recreate the table.) Naming constraints makes error messages clearer.

Relationship design

One-to-many

One customer → many orders. Put the foreign key on the "many" side: orders.customer_id.

Many-to-many

One order has many products; one product appears in many orders. You need a junction table in between: order_items(order_id, product_id, qty), with two foreign keys and a composite primary key. Other examples: students ↔ courses (enrollments), posts ↔ tags (post_tags).

CREATE TABLE tags (
  id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE product_tags (
  product_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  tag_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES tags(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  PRIMARY KEY (product_id, tag_id)
);

One-to-one

One user ↔ one profile. Use a foreign key that's also UNIQUE (or the primary key itself). Often it's simpler to keep the columns in one table.

Common mistakes

  • No foreign keys "for speed", then years of orphaned and inconsistent data.
  • Natural keys (email, phone) as primary keys.
  • Duplicate checks only in code, instead of UNIQUE.
  • CASCADE everywhere, so one mistaken delete wipes related history.
  • **Forgetting PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON** in SQLite.

Exercise

  1. Create the reviews table and test each failing insert above.
  2. Add a CHECK so product stock can never be negative (on a new test table).
  3. Design tables for students, courses and enrollments (with an enrollment date), including all keys.
  4. Decide the ON DELETE behaviour for: comments when a post is deleted; invoices when a customer is deleted. Explain why.

Summary

  • Constraints make the database enforce data rules: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT.
  • Foreign keys keep relationships valid; ON DELETE decides what happens to children.
  • UNIQUE is the reliable way to prevent duplicates.
  • One-to-many uses a foreign key; many-to-many uses a junction table.

Next, you'll make queries fast with indexes.
item.excerpt:encoded: Protect data quality with PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT constraints, choose ON DELETE behaviour, and design one-to-many and many-to-many relationships.

item.title: SQL Indexes
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
With 7 products, every query is instant. With 7 million, a query that scans every row can take seconds, and a busy website runs thousands of queries a minute. Indexes let the database find rows without reading the whole table. They're the single biggest tool for database performance.

The book index analogy

To find "foreign keys" in a 500-page book, you don't read every page. You check the index at the back: "foreign keys … page 312". A database index works the same way: a separate, sorted structure that maps column values to the rows that contain them.

Without an index, the database does a full table scan: it checks every row. With one, it jumps almost straight to the matches, even in a table with millions of rows.

Creating an index

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);
  • idx_orders_customer_id is the index's name (a common convention: idx_table_column).
  • ON orders (customer_id) says which table and column.

Queries filtering, joining or sorting on customer_id can now use it:

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1;

You don't change your queries; the database decides automatically when an index helps.

Indexes you already have

  • Every PRIMARY KEY is indexed automatically.
  • Every UNIQUE constraint creates an index (that's how the database checks uniqueness quickly).
  • Foreign keys are indexed automatically in MySQL (InnoDB), but not in PostgreSQL or SQLite. Index them yourself there, because joins use them constantly.

Seeing the query plan with EXPLAIN

EXPLAIN shows how the database will run a query:

-- SQLite:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';
-- SCAN orders                      ← full table scan

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders (status);

EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';
-- SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_status (status=?)   ← uses the index

In MySQL and PostgreSQL, write EXPLAIN SELECT …. Look for "full scan" / "Seq Scan" / "type: ALL" on big tables: that's where indexes help. PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the query and shows real timings.

(On tiny tables, databases often choose a scan anyway, because it's faster than using the index.)

What to index

Index columns that appear often in:

  • WHERE filters: WHERE email = ?, WHERE status = ?.
  • JOIN conditions: foreign keys like orders.customer_id, order_items.product_id.
  • ORDER BY: ORDER BY created_at DESC on large tables (latest posts, newest orders).

Start from real slow queries. Most databases can log slow queries (MySQL's slow query log, PostgreSQL's pg_stat_statements).

Composite indexes and column order

An index can cover several columns:

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_date ON orders (customer_id, order_date);

It's sorted by customer_id first, then by order_date within each customer, like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name. It helps:

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1;                                -- yes (first column)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 AND order_date >= '2024-05-05'; -- yes, both columns
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 ORDER BY order_date DESC;       -- yes, even the sort
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2024-05-05';                     -- no (not the first column)

This is the leftmost prefix rule: an index can be used for its first column, or first two, and so on, but not for a later column on its own. Put the column used for equality (=) first and range or sort columns after it.

When indexes can't be used

-- Function on the column: the index on email can't be used
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE LOWER(email) = 'asha@example.com';

-- Leading wildcard: like searching a phone book for names ending in "-sharma"
SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%lamp';

-- These CAN use an index:
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = 'asha@example.com';
SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'Desk%';

Store data in a consistent form (e.g. emails lower-cased on insert) so you can compare directly. PostgreSQL and MySQL 8 also support expression indexes, such as an index on LOWER(email). For searching words inside text, use full-text search.

Unique indexes

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_customers_email ON customers (email);

An index that also enforces uniqueness, the same as a UNIQUE constraint.

The cost of indexes

Indexes aren't free:

  • Slower writes: every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must also update every index on the table.
  • Disk space: each index is a copy of its columns, sorted.
  • Maintenance: unused indexes still cost on every write.

So don't index every column. Index what your queries actually need, and remove indexes nobody uses.

Indexes in WordPress

WordPress's wp_posts table has indexes on post_name (slug lookups), on (post_type, post_status, post_date, ID) for listing posts, and on post_author. That's why loading a post by its URL stays fast even with thousands of posts. Plugins that search unindexed meta values (wp_postmeta.meta_value) are a common cause of slow WordPress sites.

Removing an index

DROP INDEX idx_orders_status;              -- SQLite / PostgreSQL
-- DROP INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders; -- MySQL

Common mistakes

  • No index on foreign keys in PostgreSQL/SQLite, making joins slow.
  • Indexing everything, slowing down every write.
  • Wrong column order in composite indexes.
  • Wrapping indexed columns in functions in WHERE.
  • Guessing instead of measuring with EXPLAIN.

Exercise

  1. Run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN (SQLite) or EXPLAIN on SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE product_id = 1. Then create an index and compare.
  2. Create a composite index on orders (status, order_date). Which of these could use it: filter by status; by status and date; by date only?
  3. List the indexes you'd add to the shop database, and explain each one.
  4. Rewrite WHERE LOWER(city) = 'pune' so it could use an index on city.

Summary

  • Indexes are sorted lookup structures that avoid full table scans.
  • Primary keys and UNIQUE columns are indexed automatically; index foreign keys yourself where needed.
  • Composite indexes follow the leftmost prefix rule; order the columns carefully.
  • Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes; measure with EXPLAIN.

Next, you'll design and query a complete library database in the SQL project.
